demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
keep mind occupied all the time
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.explanation: The threat items are centered on assault/home-intrusion danger (noticing weapons, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of unexpected death of a loved one. Hypervigilance alone could fit PTSD broadly, but these two specific items imply a different trauma context.

Drop Responsibilities is framed as giving up responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers. In this profile, the listed triggers node is absent and the rest of the profile is dominated by grief/loss-linked appraisals and memory disturbance rather than a coherent pattern of situational avoidance for physical safety. That makes this specific strategy item poorly matched to the other selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring implies an ongoing interpersonal/home-invasion danger context. For trauma type of unexpected death of a loved one, this is hard to reconcile unless additional assault-related trauma is present. It also sits poorly with the formulation because Triggers→Threat is inactive, yet the threat content is highly specific to external intrusion rather than generalized post-loss threat.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is more consistent with trauma involving personal failure, assault, or injury than bereavement-focused PTSD. After unexpected death of a loved one, appraisals would more plausibly center on guilt, loss, permanent change, or the world being unsafe. 'I am a weak person' and 'I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me' are not impossible, but together they pull toward a different trauma formulation and are weakly anchored to the rest of the profile.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, the memory profile is largely grief/intrusion based, but 'Rage on Recall' stands out as difficult to reconcile with the rest of this profile because no other items indicate anger-focused appraisals, perpetrator blame, or threat-related meaning that would explain intense rage as the dominant recall response.

The Threat items describe a sustained current-danger state ('superalert', 'constantly tense and ready to react to danger'), but the formulation contains no active links into Threat and the other selected nodes are centered on loss, permanent change, numbing, and intrusive fragmented memory. This level of ongoing danger-readiness is not well integrated with the rest of the profile and appears clinically disconnected rather than supported by the appraisals or memory content.

vignette:
Amara Osei is a 33-year-old Ghanaian-American woman who works as a park ranger at a large state nature reserve in the Pacific Northwest. She came to her first session eight weeks after the sudden death of her younger brother, Kofi, who collapsed from an undetected cardiac arrhythmia while the two of them were hiking together on a trail she had personally recommended. She had been leading the way, perhaps thirty yards ahead, when she heard him fall. By the time she reached him and radioed for emergency services, Kofi was unresponsive. She performed CPR until the rescue team arrived, but he could not be revived. He was twenty-nine years old.

In the weeks that followed, Amara described the event as something that had lodged itself inside her not as a continuous memory but as a series of arrested images - the particular angle of afternoon light through the Douglas firs, the sound of his body hitting the trail, the colour of his jacket against the dirt. These fragments surfaced without invitation: in the middle of a conversation with her husband, while filling out an incident report at the ranger station, while standing at the kitchen sink. Each image arrived with the quality of a photograph rather than a moving scene, vivid and fixed, and when she tried to place them in sequence they resisted her. Alongside the intrusions came a grief so acute during those moments of recall that she described it as physically winding her - a sensation she found both overwhelming and bewildering, as though the loss were happening again each time.

Her body had not settled since the day Kofi died. She lay awake most nights, alert to every sound in the house, her muscles tense in a way that had become so habitual she no longer noticed it until her husband pointed out that she was clenching her jaw at dinner. The sleeplessness compounded a broader emotional flatness that frightened her perhaps more than anything else. She had come to believe that she was no longer the person she had been before - that something essential had been altered beyond repair. What she described as feeling dead inside was not depression in the way she understood the word; it was more like a disconnection from her own interior life, a silence where there used to be feeling.

This sense of permanent damage was sharpened by her work. Amara had spent nine years as a ranger, and her competence in the field had been central to how she understood herself. She knew trails, weather, risk, terrain. She had guided hundreds of visitors safely. Yet she had been unable to save her brother on a trail she knew by heart, and she had come to believe, with a certainty she could not argue herself out of, that she was no longer capable of the things that had defined her. She began leaving patrol routes early, citing administrative tasks, and delegating field responsibilities to junior colleagues. Her supervisor had noticed. A formal check-in had been scheduled.

At home, she kept herself occupied at all times - podcasts while cooking, television she did not watch but needed on, her phone in her hand during any unstructured moment. She had come to avoid stillness with a deliberateness she recognised as effortful but could not relinquish, because quiet felt like an opening through which the images and the grief could rush in unchecked. She had stopped the evening walks she and her husband used to take, stopped the Saturday morning calls with her mother in Accra, let her garden go unattended. Her husband, patient and worried in equal measure, had begun to ask questions she did not know how to answer.

What finally brought Amara to seek help was a conversation with her husband in which he told her, gently, that he felt he had lost her too. She sat with that for several days before calling a therapist. She arrived at the first session carrying a guilt she could barely articulate and a shame she had not yet named, and what she said she most feared was that the woman she had been before that afternoon on the trail was simply gone. What she most hoped, though she said it quietly and without much conviction, was that someone might tell her otherwise.
